name: Polynucleotide eye treatment (Plenhyl, Rejuran Healer)
lead: Polynucleotide (PN) eye treatment is a skin-booster procedure in which a clinician places tiny injections of purified DNA fragments, usually derived from salmon or trout, into the thin skin under and around the eyes. People use it to improve skin thickness, hydration and texture, with dark circles, fine lines and crepey skin as the main targets, without adding the volume of a filler.[1][2]

Rejuran, made by PharmaResearch in South Korea, is the best-known brand; Plinest (Mastelli, Italy) is another.[1] Rejuran I is sold for the under-eye area and Rejuran Healer for the face, according to clinic sources.[2]

Published research on the periorbital area includes randomised split-face trials against hyaluronic acid filler, a 2022 trial in 27 people, and a 2026 systematic review of six studies reporting short-term improvement in crow's feet grades and a favourable safety profile through six months.[4][5][6]

chain: Micro-injections of polynucleotides placed in thin eye-area skin
Fibroblasts and hydration are reported to improve
angle.text: Clients seek it for thin, crepey under-eye skin and dark circles. Providers describe it as improving skin quality without adding volume.

paras: Polynucleotides and PDRN are purified DNA fragments prepared by repeated filtration to remove cellular material, proteins and potential allergens, leaving a sterile injectable.[1] Providers say they activate fibroblasts, support collagen and elastin, attract water, calm inflammation and aid barrier repair.[1]
Under-eye versions are described as having a thinner consistency suited to the delicate area, and are given by micro-injection after numbing cream.[2]

Appointments take about 30 minutes.[2] Providers describe glow improving within one to two weeks and deeper changes over four to eight weeks.[1] Small bumps at injection sites last 24 to 48 hours, a little longer under the eyes.[1]

A 2026 review comparing the two describes hyaluronic acid as better for structural volume correction under the eyes, and polynucleotides as showing consistent gains in dermal quality, including elasticity, hydration and fine lines, with a favourable safety profile; the authors note heterogeneous study designs and call for standardised protocols and direct comparative trials.[7]

A 2022 randomised, double-blind, split-face trial in 27 people compared polynucleotide filler with non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid around the eyes, with three injections two weeks apart. Overall aesthetic scores did not differ significantly between sides; polynucleotides produced greater improvements in roughness and pore volume, improvement in elasticity and hydration faded over time in both groups with a higher rate for polynucleotides, and no serious adverse events were reported.[5]

A 2026 systematic review of six studies (five randomised split-face trials and one case series, 350 adults, mostly women with Fitzpatrick III to V skin in Korea and Thailand) found that 40 to 70 percent of treated sides improved by at least one grade on a crow's feet scale at 12 weeks, polynucleotides were noninferior to polycaprolactone filler in two trials, and no study followed patients beyond six months; the authors call the findings preliminary.[4]

A 2026 prospective observational study of 42 patients receiving intradermal polynucleotide injections for periorbital wrinkles reported significant improvement in lower eyelid and crow's feet scores on FACE-Q questionnaires at 1, 3 and 6 months, with the greatest improvement at 3 months after two sessions and minimal adverse events.[6] A 2014 phase III trial of Rejuran against hyaluronic acid for crow's feet has been retracted.[8]
Providers also state that Rejuran and Plinest data show gains in skin thickness, elasticity and hydration, without naming the papers.[1]

Common effects are redness, swelling, bumps and mild discomfort that resolve within days.[1][2] Bruising is common in the eye area, and fish or salmon allergy is a stated contraindication in manufacturer-style guidance.
Social media popularised the "salmon DNA facial" label, which one clinician calls sensationalised.[1]

timeline.event: A phase III trial of polynucleotide filler for crow's feet is published in the Journal of Korean Medical Science and later retracted (2016).[8]
Randomised split-face trial compares polynucleotide and hyaluronic acid fillers around the eyes.[5]
Systematic review of polynucleotides in periorbital rejuvenation published.[4]

card.summary: Micro-injections of salmon-derived polynucleotides under the eyes to thicken and smooth thin, crepey skin and soften dark circles.
card.aka: Rejuran I, Rejuran Healer, PN skin booster, salmon DNA facial
card.note: Contraindicated with fish allergy; not approved as an injectable in the US.

quick.overview:
A clinician injects purified polynucleotides, usually from salmon, into the skin under the eyes. It is sought for thin, crepey skin and dark circles.

Providers describe it as improving skin thickness and hydration without adding volume. A course is usually three to four sessions.
quick.mechanism: Polynucleotides are said to stimulate fibroblasts for collagen and elastin, attract water and support the skin barrier. Glow may appear within weeks, deeper changes by four to eight weeks.
quick.risks: Redness, swelling, bumps and bruising are common and resolve in days. Fish allergy is a contraindication. No injectable polynucleotide is FDA-approved, and efficacy claims mostly come from providers.
